highlights.title: Built from the law, not opinion
highlights.text: Every guide is written from legislation, regulator guidance and official websites, which we link to, and dated so you can see when it was last checked.

highlights.title: US, UK and EU, side by side
highlights.text: Online shopping crosses borders. We set out the rules in each place together, so you can see which ones apply to you.

highlights.title: Free and independent
highlights.text: OnBusLaw is free to use. We’re not a law firm and don’t sell legal services; when you need advice, we point you to qualified, often free, help.

sections.html:
Buying, selling and creating online is governed by a patchwork of consumer law, payment rules, data protection, advertising codes and intellectual property law. OnBusLaw turns that patchwork into practical guides: what the rule is, who it protects, the deadlines that matter and where to go next.

Every page covers the United States (mainly federal law, with state differences flagged), the United Kingdom and the European Union, because the answer to “can I get my money back?” or “do I need to disclose this link?” often depends on where you, and the business, are.

• Your consumer rights online: faulty goods, late deliveries and what sellers must tell you.
  • Refunds and returns: the 14-day UK and EU cancellation right and US return policies.
  • Chargebacks and card disputes: Section 75, the Fair Credit Billing Act and unauthorised payments.
  • Scams and fraud and identity theft: warning signs, first steps and where to report.
  • Complaints and customer service: how to complain effectively and escalate.

sections.h2: For online businesses, sellers and creators
sections.html:
• The legal checklist for an online business: structure, tax, data and consumer law.
  • Terms, privacy policies and cookies: the legal pages a website needs.
  • Trademarks and copyright and takedowns: protect your brand and content.
  • Affiliate and influencer disclosure rules, including fake review bans.
  • Selling on marketplaces: suspensions, seller verification and product safety.

We start from primary sources such as legislation, regulations and regulator guidance, and link to them at the end of each guide. Pages show the date they were last updated, and time-sensitive changes are covered on our blog.

Our guides are general information, not legal advice. They can’t take account of your circumstances, and they don’t replace a qualified lawyer (an attorney or solicitor) or a free advice service where you live.

faqs.a: No. OnBusLaw is a free legal information website. We don’t give legal advice or represent anyone, and reading our guides doesn’t create a lawyer–client relationship.

faqs.q: Which countries do your guides cover?
faqs.a: The United States (mainly federal law, with state differences flagged), the United Kingdom and the European Union. Where UK nations differ, for example Scotland, we say so. EU countries can add their own national rules on top of EU law.

faqs.q: How up to date is the information?
faqs.a: Each guide shows when it was last updated and links to the official sources it relies on. Laws change, so check those sources before acting on anything important.
Some pages may include affiliate links, so a provider may pay us a commission if you sign up, at no extra cost to you. This never changes what our guides say. Read how we make money.

items.title: Refunds & returns
items.text: Cancel an order, return it and get your money back.

blocks.title: Key rules at a glance
blocks.intro: Some of the most useful rules for buying and selling online. Each one links to a full guide with the conditions and exceptions.

items.title: 14-day cancellation
items.text: Most goods and services bought online from a business can be cancelled within 14 days without giving a reason. Some exceptions apply.

items.title: Section 75 protection
items.text: Paid for something costing over £100 and up to £30,000 with a credit card? The card provider can be equally liable if the trader breaches the contract.

items.title: 60 days to dispute
items.text: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, write to your card issuer within 60 days of the statement that shows a billing error.

items.title: Faulty goods
items.text: Goods must match their description and be of satisfactory quality. In the UK, you can reject faulty goods for a full refund within 30 days.

items.title: Scam reimbursement
items.text: Since 7 October 2024, UK payment firms must reimburse most victims of bank transfer (APP) scams, up to £85,000 per claim.

items.title: Withdrawal button
items.text: Since 19 June 2026, EU online traders must offer a clearly labelled “withdraw from contract” function during the cancellation period.

items.title: ® means registered
items.text: Use ® only for a registered trademark. Claiming registration falsely is a criminal offence in the UK and can be misleading elsewhere.

items.title: Label ads upfront
items.text: Paid posts, gifts and affiliate links must be clearly disclosed, for example with “#ad”, under FTC, UK and EU rules.

blocks.title: Sorting out a problem with an online purchase

items.title: Know your rights
items.text: Find the rule that fits: cancellation, faulty goods, non-delivery or a card dispute. Note any deadlines.

items.title: Put it in writing
items.text: Contact the seller, explain what went wrong, say what you want and give a reasonable deadline. Keep copies.

items.title: Escalate if needed
items.text: Use your card provider, an ADR scheme or ombudsman, a regulator or small claims court. See how to escalate.
